sources.title: Tunnelling to Holographic Traversable Wormholes
sources.reading_scope: Sections 2.1.1-2.1.3: normalized spinors, boundary action, boundary conditions and spectrum. Equations 2.12-2.14 determine the weak-branch angle. HTML 2.16 is not used; their energy prescription is not substituted for the inherited point-split stress.
sources.role: Known free boundary coupling map, not interacting quantum switching stress

source_method: Direct primary-source reading and reuse of pinned local derivations; no new exhaustive novelty search.
novelty: No novelty acceptance. Cayley contacts, Gaussian midpoint covariances and normal ordering are established methods. The bounded matching comparison is derived explicitly for the selected projected action.

verification.spectral_comparison: Every discrepancy lies within its analytic Matsubara tail bound plus independent quadrature error allowance.

accepted_scope: Weak-branch free boundary map theta=2 atan(h_boundary), with an explicit midpoint contact convention.
Initial electric projected Gaussian normalization has a common-regulator finite limit with 0<=Delta W<=beta/(8 I0).
Relative-boundary factor and initial physical/global clock match the charged strip reference ultraviolet coefficient.
Candidate midpoint exponent is below 1/(48 k) on the returned-switch z0 interval.
limitations: Initial noncompact Gaussian comparison on the fixed exterior; not the full compact charge-spin TFD.
No general microscopic finite vertex normalization or full angular/coset factorization.
A midpoint amplitude bound is not a driven energy, dephasing or switching-stress bound.
No physical preparation, general stability, finite-energy transport or topology-creation result.
remaining_todo: Determine the joint compact/angular and microscopic boundary-vertex matching.
Control the driven state and complete renormalized stress with common subtraction, mixed current correlations and evolving geometry.
Compare errors against the capture and area margins; establish preparation, quantum fluctuations, sufficient stability and finite-energy transport.
